evidence.claim: These are working transportation links: the Southeast network combines mainline voyages typically lasting more than a day with shorter routes whose boats return to their home ports the same day.
evidence.quote: the mainline routes which typically take more than one day for the ship to travel; and shorter routes where the vessels depart their home port in the morning, travel to destination ports and then return to their home port on the same day.

evidence.claim: The network began with a much smaller connection: in 1948, Haines residents Steve Homer and Ray Gelotte founded Chilkoot Motorship Lines.
evidence.quote: The forerunner to the Alaska Marine Highway was the Chilkoot Motorship Lines, founded in 1948 by Haines residents Steve Homer and Ray Gelotte.

evidence.claim: Their converted landing craft ran weekly from Tee Harbor to Haines and Skagway, linking the territorial capital with the international road system.
evidence.quote: The company used a converted LCT-Mark VI landing craft, christened the MV Chilkoot. They operated a weekly service from Tee Harbor (north of Juneau) to Haines and Skagway, connecting the territorial capital to the international road system.

evidence.claim: The territory bought the line in 1951; in 1959, voters approved an $18 million bond package for vessels and docks.
evidence.quote: The Chilkoot Motorship Lines was purchased by the territorial government, and moved under the Territorial Board of Road Commissioners in 1951.

evidence.claim: The territory bought the line in 1951; in 1959, voters approved an $18 million bond package for vessels and docks.
evidence.quote: In 1959, the year Alaska became a state, voters approved an $18 million ($199 million today) bond package to improve the ferry system throughout the Southeast and Southcentral regions. The package included 4 new vessels and new docks throughout.

evidence.claim: The southern terminus moved from Seattle to Bellingham in 1989.
evidence.quote: The southern terminus of the AMHS remained in Seattle until October 1989, when it moved to the Bellingham Cruise Terminal in Fairhaven, Washington

evidence.claim: Follow the Inside Passage portion south from Skagway through Haines and Juneau, then Petersburg, Wrangell and Ketchikan toward Bellingham.
evidence.quote: The mainline routes carry a high percentage of tourists in the summer, and provide service between Bellingham, Washington, or Prince Rupert, British Columbia, and Skagway, Alaska. Along the way, the ships stop in Ketchikan, Wrangell, Petersburg, Sitka, Juneau, and Haines.

evidence.claim: Skagway’s port stands at the beginning of a railway built during the Klondike gold rush.
evidence.quote: The White Pass and Yukon Route narrow gauge railroad, part of the area's mining past, now in operation purely for the tourist trade and running throughout the summer months, has its starting point at the port of Skagway.

evidence.claim: On July 29, 1897, the steamer Queen brought the first boatload of prospectors to Moore’s wharf.
evidence.quote: On July 29, 1897, the steamer Queen docked at Moore's wharf with the first boat load of prospectors.

evidence.claim: The White Pass and Yukon Route began laying narrow-gauge tracks in May 1898.
evidence.quote: It was not until May 1898 that the White Pass and Yukon Route began laying narrow gauge railroad tracks in Skagway.

evidence.claim: By the time the railroad was completed in 1900, the rush was nearly over.
evidence.quote: By 1900, when the railroad was completed, the gold rush was nearly over.

evidence.claim: The town occupies a narrow glaciated valley at the head of Taiya Inlet.
evidence.quote: Skagway is located in a narrow glaciated valley at the head of the Taiya Inlet

evidence.claim: Its historic district contains about 100 gold-rush-era buildings.
evidence.quote: Skagway has a historical district of about 100 buildings from the gold rush era.

evidence.claim: The White Pass and Yukon Route now runs narrow-gauge passenger trains from the port during the summer months.
evidence.quote: The White Pass and Yukon Route narrow gauge railroad, part of the area's mining past, now in operation purely for the tourist trade and running throughout the summer months, has its starting point at the port of Skagway.

evidence.claim: Icebergs from LeConte Glacier once supplied Petersburg’s fishing port with ice to cool its catch.
evidence.quote: Icebergs from the nearby LeConte Glacier provided a source for cooling fish.

evidence.claim: In the nineteenth century, Norwegian immigrant Peter Buschmann built a cannery, sawmill and docks here; the settlement took his name.
evidence.quote: In the 19th century, Peter Buschmann, a Norwegian immigrant, settled here, building a cannery, sawmill, docks and early structures. The settlement was named Petersburg after him, and it flourished as a fishing port.

evidence.claim: Scandinavian immigration gave the town its nickname, Little Norway.
evidence.quote: The town had attracted mostly immigrants of Scandinavian origin, thus giving Petersburg the nickname "Little Norway".

evidence.claim: Petersburg celebrates Norwegian Constitution Day with Mayfest on the third weekend in May.
evidence.quote: Petersburg celebrates Norwegian Constitution Day in a celebration called "Mayfest," on the third weekend in May.

evidence.claim: Commercial fishing remains the main driver of the economy.
evidence.quote: Commercial fishing is the dominant economic driver of Petersburg's economy.

evidence.claim: The town sits at the north end of Mitkof Island, where Wrangell Narrows meets Frederick Sound.
evidence.quote: Petersburg is located on the north end of Mitkof Island, where the Wrangell Narrows meets Frederick Sound.

evidence.claim: It is also the headquarters of the Petersburg Indian Association, a federally recognized tribe of Tlingit people.
evidence.quote: The town is the headquarters of the Petersburg Indian Association, a federally recognized tribe of Tlingit people.

evidence.claim: Whales, salmon and faces appear in carvings on Wrangell’s shore.
evidence.quote: They depict whales, salmon, and faces of the community.

evidence.claim: At Petroglyph Beach, barely a mile out of town, at least 40 petroglyphs have been found.
evidence.quote: Located on the shore of Wrangell, Alaska barely a mile out of town, it became a State Historic Park in 2000. At least 40 petroglyphs have been found to date.

evidence.claim: They occupy boulders and bedrock outcrops just above and below mean high tide.
evidence.quote: The petroglyphs that remain here are found on the boulders and bedrock outcrops on the shore, just below and above mean high tide.

evidence.claim: The carvings are thought to have been made by members of the Tlingit tribe.
evidence.quote: It is thought that they were created by members of the Tlingit tribe

evidence.claim: The beach became a State Historic Park in 2000.
evidence.quote: it became a State Historic Park in 2000.

evidence.claim: Alaska’s transportation department identifies it as Southeast Alaska’s highest concentration of petroglyphs.
evidence.quote: View the highest concentration of petroglyphs in Southeast Alaska in Wrangell at Petroglyph Beach State Historic Park .

evidence.claim: The metamorphic rock tends to be dark gray and finely grained; Wikipedia suggests that its ease of fracture would have helped the carvers work it.
evidence.quote: The rock here is metamorphic and tends to be a dark gray that is finely grained, moderately durable, and easy to fracture, which would make it easier to manipulate for petroglyphs.

evidence.claim: Look for carved figures on shore boulders and bedrock above and below mean high tide.
evidence.quote: The petroglyphs that remain here are found on the boulders and bedrock outcrops on the shore, just below and above mean high tide.
